meta.label: Razors & shaving
meta.attribution: Curated from public product materials, blade/recycling program pages, B Corp profiles, and waste references - not lab-measured. The core trade-off is durable metal tools and cheap replaceable blades versus convenient mixed-material cartridges/disposables. Reviewed 2026-06. Suggest changes via Contribute.

products.name: Safety razor (double-edge metal)

environment.note: Double-edge safety razors replace plastic cartridges with small steel blades that can be collected for scrap recycling.

durability.note: Safety-razor model is a reusable metal handle rather than a disposable plastic body.

economical.note: Replacement double-edge blades are low cost; Henson lists 100 blades for $9.99 and says that lasts typical shavers 2-3 years.

ethics.note: Maker ethics vary widely; the value is mostly the durable, non-proprietary format rather than any one certification.

accessibility.note: There is a real technique/angle learning curve, but DE blades are non-proprietary and widely sold.

products.description: A classic double-edge metal safety razor is the simplest low-waste shave: keep the handle, replace only the thin steel blade.

products.name: Leaf / pivoting safety razor

environment.note: Leaf says its plastic-free razors use recyclable steel blades that can be recycled locally or sent back.

durability.note: Leaf uses durable handles and replaceable steel blades rather than disposable plastic cartridges.

economical.note: Leaf blade refills are much cheaper per shave than proprietary cartridge heads after the handle purchase.

ethics.note: Sustainability-focused design and recycling support, but no B Corp certification found during this review.

accessibility.note: Pivoting head and guarded blades make it easier for cartridge users than a rigid classic safety razor.

products.description: A pivoting-head metal razor that uses standard safety blades, aiming to make the plastic-free switch feel closer to a cartridge shave.

products.name: Bamboo-handled safety razor

environment.note: Bambaw says one durable razor replaces hundreds of disposable ones and uses recyclable Swedish steel blades.

durability.note: Bamboo-handled versions are reusable, but wood/bamboo handles can be less lifetime-durable than full stainless models.

economical.note: Bambaw says a 100-blade pack can last years depending on shave frequency and hair type.

ethics.note: Eco-focused packaging and non-proprietary blade model, with no broad third-party governance certification found.

accessibility.note: Available online and through eco retailers, but not as instant or familiar as supermarket cartridges.

products.description: A bamboo or mixed-material safety razor keeps the low-waste blade model while swapping some handle material away from all-metal.

products.name: Straight razor

environment.note: A maintained straight razor uses no disposable cartridge or replaceable blade waste during normal use.

durability.note: DOVO says a straight razor is not disposable and can last for generations.

economical.note: Running cost is low after the razor/strop/honing setup, but maintenance tools and sharpening matter.

ethics.note: Often made by specialist craft manufacturers, but ethics depends on maker and materials.

accessibility.note: Requires careful technique plus regular stropping/honing, making it much less accessible for casual shaving.

products.description: The lowest-consumable option if you can maintain it: one blade, stropping/honing, and a steep skill curve.

products.name: Precision metal safety razor (e.g. Henson)

environment.note: Henson AL13 is an all-metal double-edge safety razor using small stainless steel blades rather than plastic cartridges.

durability.note: Henson positions the AL13 as aircraft aluminum with a reusable handle and replaceable DE blades.

economical.note: A listed 100-pack of Henson/RK blades costs $9.99 and is described as lasting typical shavers 2-3 years.

ethics.note: Independent durable-product maker with cruelty-free skincare line, but no B Corp-style certification found.

accessibility.note: Designed to reduce blade chatter and irritation, but still requires learning safety-razor technique.

products.description: A precision-machined safety razor that keeps the cheap double-edge blade model but is designed to feel calmer for beginners.

products.name: MERKUR 34C safety razor

environment.note: MERKUR 34C is a reusable two-piece safety razor using replaceable double-edge blades rather than plastic cartridges.

durability.note: Official materials list brass handle, diecast zinc head, galvanized surfaces and bright chrome plating.

economical.note: The 34C uses the standard safety-razor format, avoiding proprietary cartridge refill pricing after the handle purchase.

ethics.note: Long-lived German-made tool with conventional manufacturer transparency, but no broad mission-led certification found.

accessibility.note: MERKUR sells the 34C through its EU shop and points US/Canadian customers to North American support, but it still requires safety-razor technique.

products.description: A benchmark Solingen-made double-edge safety razor: less plastic and strong long-run value, with a real technique curve.

products.name: Hanni Weighted Razor

environment.note: Hanni says the weighted razor is 100% metal/plastic-free and uses recyclable Swedish stainless steel blades.

durability.note: The product page describes a powder-coated all-metal razor with body-shaving grip features and reusable handle design.

economical.note: Hanni blades are proprietary and listed at $6 for a 5-pack, so costs are lower-waste but not as cheap as standard DE blades.

ethics.note: Hanni publishes packaging standards, FSC/SGP paper packaging claims, plastic-reduction goals and impact metrics.

accessibility.note: Body-oriented design may feel easier than some safety razors, but the razor depends on Hanni-specific blades and product availability.

products.description: A body-shaving metal razor that reduces plastic and improves grip, but trades standard DE blade economics for proprietary blades.

products.name: Electric razor (rechargeable)

environment.note: Electric shavers avoid frequent disposable blade waste, but Earth911 flags their metals, plastics, batteries and e-waste footprint.

durability.note: Major brands sell replacement heads; Philips recommends replacing many shaver heads every 12 months for performance.

economical.note: Higher upfront device price plus periodic replacement heads, but no cartridge purchase every few shaves.

ethics.note: EPA says electronics contain valuable materials and batteries should be recycled separately, so repair/recycling access matters for this mainstream category.

accessibility.note: Easy, familiar, and widely sold with lower cut risk than exposed blades for many users.

products.description: A rechargeable electric shaver avoids daily blade/cartridge waste, but it is an electronic device with batteries and replacement heads.

products.name: Philips Norelco OneBlade

environment.note: OneBlade avoids frequent disposable cartridges but remains a rechargeable device with proprietary replacement heads.

durability.note: Philips says each OneBlade blade lasts about four months on average, depending on routine.

economical.note: Replacement heads last longer than disposable razors but cost more than safety-razor blades.

ethics.note: Mainstream electronics ownership gives limited mission-led signal, and batteries/e-waste remain end-of-life concerns.

accessibility.note: Widely sold and easy to use wet or dry, making it one of the most accessible lower-blade-waste electric options.

products.description: OneBlade is a high-convenience electric hybrid: less cartridge churn than manual systems, but still proprietary, battery-powered, and eventually e-waste.

products.name: Albatross safety razor + blade take-back

environment.note: Albatross runs a used-blade take-back program to recycle/upcycle double-edge blades into new products.

durability.note: Reusable metal handle plus replaceable double-edge blades, rather than disposable plastic bodies.

economical.note: Uses low-cost non-proprietary double-edge blades after the upfront handle purchase.

ethics.note: Blade take-back was created because municipal recycling often does not accept used blades, giving a clear circularity practice.

accessibility.note: Online-first and requires safety-razor technique plus saving/mailing used blades.

products.description: A safety razor system with an unusually concrete circularity feature: a blade take-back program for used DE blades.

products.name: Rockwell 6S stainless safety razor

environment.note: Uses replaceable double-edge blades instead of mixed-material plastic cartridges.

durability.note: Rockwell describes the 6S as 316L stainless steel, built to last a lifetime, with lifetime warranty.

economical.note: Premium upfront purchase but uses inexpensive DE blades rather than proprietary cartridge refills.

ethics.note: Durable-product model from an independent razor maker; no broad third-party ethics certification found.

accessibility.note: Six adjustable shave settings can help fit/learning, but it remains a safety razor with technique needs.

products.description: A premium adjustable stainless-steel safety razor built for long service life and lower-cost DE blades.

products.name: Supply Single Edge razor

environment.note: Supply's single-edge system uses a long-lived metal handle and replaceable blades instead of disposable plastic bodies.

durability.note: Supply describes the SE as a solid steel handle with zinc-alloy head, built to last decades and backed by a lifetime warranty.

economical.note: Replacement blade packs lower ongoing cost versus many cartridges, though Supply's blade system is less universal than DE blades.

ethics.note: Durability is the main values signal; no broad third-party sustainability or governance certification was found.

accessibility.note: Single-edge technique and online-first refills make it less instantly accessible than drugstore cartridges.

products.description: Supply is a modern single-edge metal razor for people who want less plastic than cartridges but a more guided feel than classic DE razors.

products.name: MUEHLE Companion safety razor

environment.note: MUEHLE says safety razors use recyclable metal blades and plastic-free/paper packaging compared with disposable razors.

durability.note: MUEHLE frames its safety razors as high-quality tools that remain reliable companions for years.

economical.note: The razor takes traditional double-edge blades, avoiding proprietary cartridge refill pricing.

ethics.note: MUEHLE publishes sustainability practices around recyclable packaging and reduced plastic shipping materials.

accessibility.note: Companion is designed as a gentler body/face safety razor, but it still requires blade handling and technique.

products.description: MUEHLE Companion is a polished unisex DE safety razor that broadens the reusable option set beyond US startup brands.

products.name: Bevel Safety Razor

environment.note: Bevel uses a reusable brass handle and replaceable double-edge blades instead of whole disposable plastic razors.

durability.note: Bevel describes the razor as a brass weighted tool designed to avoid the cheap feel and lifetime cost of disposables.

economical.note: Higher upfront than disposables but ships with blades and uses non-proprietary DE-style refills rather than cartridge packs.

ethics.note: Bevel centers shaving needs often underserved by multi-blade systems, especially coarse hair and razor-bump concerns.

accessibility.note: Bevel is sold direct and through Target, but safety-razor blade handling still makes it less plug-and-play than cartridges.

products.description: A brass single-blade safety razor that adds a mainstream-retail reusable option, especially for users trying to avoid multi-blade irritation.

products.name: Bambaw safety razor

environment.note: Bambaw frames safety razors as plastic-free alternatives to disposable plastic razors and cartridges.

durability.note: Bambaw describes safety razors as stainless-steel tools designed to last a lifetime.

economical.note: The razor uses standard double-edge blades; Bambaw sells stainless blade refills instead of proprietary cartridges.

ethics.note: Bambaw emphasizes plastic-free design and sustainable packaging, but no broad third-party governance certification was found.

accessibility.note: Available online and through many European independent retailers, but still less familiar than drugstore cartridges.

products.description: A plastic-free safety-razor option with standard DE blades and strong waste credentials, though it still asks users to learn blade handling.

products.name: King C. Gillette safety razor

environment.note: A double-edge metal handle avoids mixed-material cartridge heads, though it is sold by a mainstream disposable/cartridge brand.

durability.note: Product listings describe a chrome-plated handle with replaceable double-edge blades rather than a disposable razor body.

economical.note: Uses inexpensive double-edge blades, making long-run cost far lower than proprietary cartridge refills.

ethics.note: P&G/Gillette ownership is mainstream, but the format itself meaningfully reduces cartridge waste and lock-in.

accessibility.note: Much easier to find than boutique safety razors through Amazon and mass retail, while still requiring DE technique.

products.description: A useful bridge option: a mainstream-brand safety razor that makes DE shaving more accessible without solving P&G/Gillette ethics concerns.

products.name: Preserve POPi recycled-plastic razor

environment.note: POPi handles use recycled ocean-bound plastic, but the system still depends on disposable multi-blade cartridges.

durability.note: Handle is reusable/recyclable through Preserve mail-in, while replacement cartridges are disposable.

economical.note: Mid-priced cartridge system: less cheap long-run than DE blades, often cheaper/easier than premium cartridges.

ethics.note: Preserve is a Certified B Corp centered on recycled consumer goods and reduced-impact products.

accessibility.note: Available online and through some mainstream retail; easier than safety razors for cartridge users.

products.description: A more conventional cartridge feel with a recycled-plastic handle and B Corp maker, though cartridges remain the weak point.

products.name: Cartridge razor + mail-in recycling

environment.note: TerraCycle/Gillette accepts blades, razors, and plastic packaging from all brands, but requires special collection and shipping.

durability.note: The underlying product is still a disposable cartridge or disposable razor stream.

economical.note: Recycling program may be free/sponsored, but proprietary cartridges remain expensive compared with DE blades.

ethics.note: Better end-of-life option from a mainstream brand partnership, but not the same as waste prevention.

accessibility.note: Useful where program access exists, but users must dry, store, package, and ship/drop off items.

products.description: A harm-reduction route for cartridge users: keep the familiar shave, then collect and mail back hard-to-recycle razors.

products.name: Plastic-free shave soap bar (e.g. Badger)

environment.note: Badger shave bar avoids aerosol cans and plastic shave-gel bottles with solid bar format.

durability.note: Concentrated bar/puck format lasts across many shaves, especially with a reusable dish/brush routine.

economical.note: Moderate upfront price but slow use-down compared with single-use foams; value depends on lather routine.

ethics.note: Badger is a Certified B Corp; product page states vegan, cruelty-free, plastic-free/recyclable packaging and solar-powered production.

accessibility.note: Available online and some natural-products retail, but solid soap requires a slightly different shaving routine.

products.description: A solid shave bar cuts packaging waste around the shaving routine, though it does not solve razor/blade waste by itself.

products.name: Estrid Body Razor

environment.note: Estrid uses a stainless-steel handle, but the system still depends on disposable five-blade cartridges.

durability.note: Estrid says its steel handle is built to withstand repeated use and is covered by a lifetime guarantee.

economical.note: Estrid sells a low-priced starter kit and recurring blade refills, cheaper than some cartridges but far above standard DE blade costs.

ethics.note: Estrid says it is a completely vegan company and that its lubrication strip is 100% cruelty-free.

accessibility.note: Available across multiple European countries with flexible subscription, pause and cancel controls, but not a global retail default.

products.description: A European cartridge subscription with a reusable steel handle and stronger vegan/cruelty-free signals, though cartridge waste remains.

products.name: FFS Beauty razor + blade recycling

environment.note: FFS runs a blade return program that grinds returned blades and separates metal and plastic for recycling.

durability.note: FFS is still a refill-cartridge system with a reusable handle, not a non-proprietary safety razor.

economical.note: Subscription refills add convenience but remain costlier long-run than standard safety-razor blades.

ethics.note: FFS says it was the first razor refill plan brand to offer blade recycling and that all packaging is recyclable.

accessibility.note: UK delivery subscription lets users skip, pause or cancel, but blade recycling requires saving and posting used FFS blades back.

products.description: A UK cartridge subscription with a real used-blade return route: better end-of-life than ordinary cartridges, but still not source reduction.

products.name: Billie razor

environment.note: Billie uses a reusable handle with refill cartridges, but the 5-blade heads remain mixed-material disposable waste.

durability.note: The handle is reusable and the magnetic holder keeps blades dry, while cartridges are replaced on a subscription cadence.

economical.note: Billie sells a $10 starter kit and four refill blades for $10, cheaper than many premium cartridges but far above DE blades.

ethics.note: Billie has stronger body-positive and cruelty-free signals than many mainstream cartridges, but no low-waste certification.

accessibility.note: Direct subscription and retail visibility make Billie highly accessible for cartridge users.

products.description: Billie is a recognizable subscription cartridge option: good access and price messaging, but still a disposable cartridge system.

products.name: Athena Club razor

environment.note: Athena Club uses a refillable cartridge model with a built-to-last aluminum handle, but blade cartridges are still disposable.

durability.note: The razor kit page describes a built-to-last aluminum handle with replaceable five-blade refills.

economical.note: Athena Club lists refill plans around $2.50-$3.00 per blade, cheaper than some premium cartridges but costly versus DE blades.

ethics.note: Athena Club FAQ says items are never tested on animals, and its ingredients page avoids animal-derived ingredients.

accessibility.note: Subscription plus Walmart/Target retail availability makes it an easy cartridge alternative for US shoppers.

products.description: Athena Club improves handle durability and cruelty-free signals within a familiar cartridge subscription model.

products.name: Flamingo razor

environment.note: Flamingo uses a reusable handle and some recycled plastic in the handle, but 5-blade cartridges are still mixed-material waste.

durability.note: Flamingo sells replaceable 5-blade cartridges compatible with reusable handles, not whole disposable razors.

economical.note: Flamingo lists cartridge packs around $2.00-$2.50 per cartridge depending pack size/subscription, cheaper than many premium cartridges but not DE-cheap.

ethics.note: Recycled-plastic handle content is a modest improvement, but no broad low-waste or third-party governance certification was found.

accessibility.note: Flamingo is widely sold through Target, grocery, and direct channels, making it easy to find for cartridge users.

products.description: Flamingo is an easy retail cartridge step above throwaway disposables, but its environmental ceiling is limited by mixed-material refills.

products.name: Gillette Venus Extra Smooth razor

environment.note: Venus Extra Smooth uses a reusable handle, but its 5-blade cartridge refills remain mixed-material disposable heads.

durability.note: Venus describes the handle as refillable and compatible with replacement cartridge blades, not whole disposable razors.

economical.note: Proprietary Venus refill cartridges are more expensive long-run than standard double-edge blades despite the reusable handle.

ethics.note: The Gillette/TerraCycle program accepts blades, razors, and plastic packaging, but mail-in recycling is still a special program rather than default curbside circularity.

accessibility.note: Venus is broadly sold through US mass retail, drugstores, and online channels with many refill options.

products.description: A very accessible body-shaving cartridge system: better than whole disposables, but locked into mixed-material proprietary refills.

products.name: Schick Hydro Silk razor

environment.note: Hydro Silk includes refillable options, but replacement cartridges are still mixed-material disposable blade heads.

durability.note: Schick's product information lists refill formats for Hydro Silk handles, improving reuse compared with whole disposables.

economical.note: Reusable handles avoid buying a whole razor each time, but proprietary Hydro Silk cartridge refills stay far above DE blade costs.

ethics.note: Schick and Skintimate launched a TerraCycle recycling program for disposable razors and packaging, but cartridge waste still needs special handling.

accessibility.note: Schick says it is sold through favorite retailers in-store and online, and Hydro Silk is a prominent mainstream product line.

products.description: A familiar refillable cartridge razor line with wide availability and some recycling-program support, but still not a low-waste shaving system.

products.name: Wilkinson Sword Hydro 5

environment.note: Hydro 5 keeps a reusable handle, but the system still depends on disposable multi-blade cartridges.

durability.note: Wilkinson Sword says all Hydro blade refills are compatible across the range and snap onto a reusable handle.

economical.note: Reusable handle improves on whole disposables, but proprietary Hydro cartridges cost far more per shave than standard DE blades.

ethics.note: Packaging claims include more than 90% recycled paper and recyclability, but blade cartridges remain special-waste items.

accessibility.note: A familiar mainstream cartridge system sold through Wilkinson Sword channels and retailers, especially in the UK/EU.

products.description: A mainstream UK/EU cartridge line: easier and less wasteful than whole disposables, but still locked into proprietary mixed-material heads.

products.name: GilletteLabs razor

environment.note: Premium GilletteLabs handles still depend on disposable five-blade cartridges, including heated/exfoliating-bar refill formats.

durability.note: The handle is reusable, but refills fit specific GilletteLabs handles and are replaced repeatedly.

economical.note: Retail listings show GilletteLabs refills costing several dollars per cartridge, far above non-proprietary DE blade packs.

ethics.note: Gillette participates in a TerraCycle razor recycling program, but that is a special mail-in route rather than low-waste design.

accessibility.note: Very widely sold premium mainstream system with strong retail availability.

products.description: GilletteLabs is the premium mainstream cartridge path: high convenience and retail access, but high refill cost and limited waste reduction.

products.name: BIC Click / Soleil refillable razors

environment.note: BIC's refillable-hybrid format keeps the handle and replaces only cartridges, but still creates cartridge waste.

durability.note: BIC describes the hybrid models as keeping the handle while replacing blade cartridges.

economical.note: Refillable cartridges reduce whole-razor repurchase, but remain a proprietary cartridge model rather than low-cost standard blades.

ethics.note: BIC cites 30% recycled plastic in the Click 3 Soleil handle and 80% recycled-cardboard packaging for this European launch.

accessibility.note: BIC's hybrid line is a familiar bridge for disposable users where the refillable models are stocked.

products.description: A bridge away from fully disposable BIC razors: the handle stays, but the proprietary plastic cartridge pattern remains.

products.name: Double-edge blade packs (Feather, Astra, Personna)

environment.note: A DE blade pack supports a reusable safety-razor handle and avoids mixed plastic cartridge heads, though used blades still need safe metal disposal.

durability.note: DE blades are consumables, but they fit many safety razors instead of locking users into one proprietary handle system.

economical.note: Rockwell lists a 100-pack of double-edge blades as about two years of shaving, making the refill model very low-cost.

ethics.note: Maker transparency varies by blade brand; Feather highlights Japanese factory control and replaceable-blade manufacturing history.

accessibility.note: DE blade packs are widely available online and in wet-shaving shops, but less common in ordinary supermarkets than cartridges.

products.description: The refill that makes safety razors economically compelling: tiny standard steel blades instead of proprietary plastic cartridge heads.

products.name: Subscription blades (Dollar Shave Club / Harry's)

environment.note: Harrys sells multi-blade cartridge refills; packaging may be recyclable but blade cartridges remain mixed-material waste.

durability.note: Durable handle plus disposable cartridge heads; not a lifetime/non-proprietary blade system.

economical.note: Harrys lists Plus blade refills around $2.81-$3.75 each depending pack size, cheaper than many premium cartridge packs but far above DE blades.

ethics.note: Harrys publishes a mental-health giving mission, but is not a low-waste or certified values-led razor system.

accessibility.note: Very convenient direct/retail/subscription model with familiar cartridge format.

products.description: Subscription cartridges improve price and convenience, but still lock users into mixed-material disposable heads.

products.name: Gillette / Schick cartridge

environment.note: Reloadable cartridges are a hard-to-recycle mix of plastic, metal blades, and packaging, typically requiring special programs.

durability.note: Handle may last, but cartridge heads are designed for repeated replacement.

economical.note: Walmart listings show Gillette Fusion refills can cost multiple dollars per cartridge, far above DE blade costs.

ethics.note: Mainstream P&G/Edgewell ownership with some recycling partnerships, but no low-waste default or mission certification.

accessibility.note: Sold almost everywhere and familiar to most shavers.

products.description: Mainstream cartridge systems are easy to find and easy to use, but costly over time and hard to recycle without special programs.

products.name: Disposable plastic razors

environment.note: Zero Waste Sonoma says mixed-material razors are hard to recycle and cites about 2 billion hard-to-recycle blades and razors discarded yearly.

durability.note: Disposable product pages explicitly advertise use-and-toss convenience rather than handle reuse.

economical.note: Low individual price but recurring replacement makes it worse long-run than reusable handles with DE blades.

ethics.note: Mainstream disposable category with little values certification and high waste by design.

accessibility.note: Highly available in grocery, drugstore, travel, and convenience retail.

products.description: The honest floor: cheapest and most available up front, but designed to be thrown away whole.

products.name: Harry's Original razor

environment.note: Harry's Original uses a reusable handle but proprietary mixed-material cartridge refills, so waste is lower than disposables but worse than DE blades.

durability.note: Blade refills are only compatible with Harry's Original handle system, meaning the handle can last but the shaving surface is designed for recurring replacement.

economical.note: Harry's advertises refill packs at lower per-cartridge prices than many premium drugstore systems, but still far above double-edge blade costs.

ethics.note: Harry's improves price competition in cartridge shaving, but the reviewed product pages do not show a low-waste, refill-recycling or third-party mission certification.

accessibility.note: Harry's is sold direct online and through mainstream retail, with simple starter sets and refills.

products.description: A convenient cartridge-subscription option that competes on price and access, but keeps users in proprietary refill cartridges.

products.name: Dollar Shave Club razor

environment.note: Dollar Shave Club uses reusable handles with cartridge refills, but the recurring mixed-material cartridge remains the main waste tradeoff.

durability.note: The company recommends replacing its Signature 6 Blade cartridge weekly, so the handle is durable but the cartridge system is not low-consumption.

economical.note: Dollar Shave Club advertises low starter and refill prices, especially with subscriptions, but still costs more long-run than standard DE blades.

ethics.note: Dollar Shave Club's main values signal is price competition and convenience, not a clear low-waste or certified ethical-maker model.

accessibility.note: Dollar Shave Club sells online subscriptions and is also available through mass retailers such as Walmart and Target.

products.description: A mainstream affordability bridge: easier and cheaper than many cartridges, but still cartridge waste and subscription friction.

products.name: Bulldog Original Bamboo Razor

environment.note: Bulldog uses a responsibly sourced bamboo handle and recycled/recyclable packaging, but it still relies on 5-blade cartridge heads.

durability.note: The bamboo handle is reusable and compatible with replacement blades, though the shaving system remains cartridge-based.

economical.note: The handle is affordable, but proprietary cartridge refills keep long-run costs above DE safety razors.

ethics.note: Bulldog states its products are cruelty-free and vegan-certified, and its China pilot preserved Leaping Bunny status.

accessibility.note: Bulldog is sold online and in mainstream grooming aisles in several markets, but not as universally as Gillette or Schick.

products.description: A better mainstream cartridge option for shoppers who want bamboo and cruelty-free signals but are not ready for safety razors.

products.name: Braun electric shaver

environment.note: A rechargeable shaver avoids daily cartridge/disposable waste, but introduces electronics, batteries and eventual e-waste.

durability.note: Braun sells replacement heads and recommends replacing the shaving head every 18 months to maintain performance.

economical.note: High upfront cost can pay off for frequent shavers because the consumable interval is measured in months rather than days or weeks.

ethics.note: Braun is a mainstream P&G appliance brand; this entry is scored mainly for durability, not for a standout ethical-maker certification.

accessibility.note: Braun shavers and replacement heads are broadly available through major retail and online channels.

products.description: A reusable electric route that can reduce cartridge waste, with the honest caveat that electronics have their own footprint.

products.name: OUI the People Single Blade Razor

environment.note: The razor is a single-blade safety razor paired with stainless-steel refills, avoiding plastic cartridge systems.

durability.note: Retail/product materials describe the handle as a weighted stainless-steel safety razor built for long-term use.

economical.note: The handle is expensive up front and the brand's 10-pack refills cost more than generic DE blade packs, so long-run value is good but not the cheapest.

ethics.note: The strongest values signal is a long-lived, lower-waste product design rather than a broad third-party ethical-maker certification.

accessibility.note: OUI the People is a premium niche body-care brand with higher upfront pricing and narrower availability than drugstore systems.

products.description: A premium single-blade safety razor for sensitive-skin shoppers who want lower waste but can absorb a high upfront price.

products.name: Kitsch Perfect Glide Safety Razor

environment.note: Kitsch describes the Perfect Glide as a plastic-free reusable safety razor with a metal handle and stainless-steel blades.

durability.note: The kit includes a reusable metal handle and separate blade refills, making it more durable than disposable or cartridge systems.

economical.note: The handle is relatively affordable for a safety razor and standard blade refills keep long-run costs lower than cartridges.

ethics.note: Kitsch product pages highlight plastic-free, reusable design and vegan/cruelty-free adjacent shave-bundle claims, but not a broad maker certification for the razor.

accessibility.note: Kitsch sells direct and through mainstream beauty retailers such as Ulta and Grove, making it easier to find than many niche safety razors.

products.description: A lower-friction safety-razor option: plastic-free and reusable, with broader beauty-retail access than many zero-waste razors.

products.name: Edwin Jagger DE89

environment.note: The DE89 is a reusable double-edge safety razor, so the recurring waste is thin DE blades rather than plastic cartridge heads.

durability.note: Edwin Jagger describes the DE89 as machined from solid brass, triple-plated, hand-polished and finished in durable chrome.

economical.note: It uses standard double-edge blades rather than proprietary cartridge heads, keeping refills low-cost after the handle purchase.

ethics.note: A long-running Sheffield wet-shaving maker with durable design, but no broad third-party social or environmental certification found for this razor.

accessibility.note: The mild closed-comb DE89 is widely sold and beginner-friendly for a safety razor, though it still requires loose-blade handling.

products.description: A classic entry-level metal safety razor with standard blades and broad wet-shaving availability.

products.name: Parker Variant Adjustable Safety Razor

environment.note: The Variant uses standard double-edge blades in a reusable handle, reducing recurring plastic waste versus cartridges.

durability.note: Parker lists the Variant as a two-piece adjustable safety razor with a genuine brass frame and premium finish.

economical.note: Standard DE blades avoid cartridge lock-in and keep ongoing blade costs low after the mid-price handle.

ethics.note: Parker describes itself as a family-owned business with a 50-year history, but no broad independent sustainability certification is shown.

accessibility.note: Adjustable settings let users tune blade exposure from mild to more aggressive, improving fit once the safety-razor technique is learned.

products.description: An adjustable double-edge razor for people who want the low-waste blade format with more control over shave aggressiveness.

products.name: RazoRock Game Changer

products.name: Karve Christopher Bradley Safety Razor

products.name: Aylsworth Apex Safety Razor

products.name: EcoRoots Safety Razor

economical.note: EcoRoots' safety razor is priced as an affordable handle and uses low-cost replacement blades.

ethics.note: EcoRoots focuses its catalog on plastic-free and zero-waste swaps, but the razor page does not show a broad third-party company certification.

products.name: UpCircle Plastic-Free Safety Razor

accessibility.note: The product is sold direct and works on face and body, but it still requires safety-razor technique.

products.name: Wild & Stone Safety Razor

environment.note: Wild & Stone describes its safety razor as plastic-free and sustainable, with recyclable eco-friendly card packaging.

durability.note: The razor is a reusable safety-razor format rather than a disposable cartridge or plastic handle.

economical.note: Standard replacement blades make long-run costs lower than proprietary cartridges once the handle is bought.

ethics.note: Wild & Stone says the safety razor is vegan and cruelty-free and describes a mission to replace common plastic products.

accessibility.note: It is a niche UK-oriented plastic-free brand and still requires the normal safety-razor learning curve.

products.description: A plastic-free reusable safety razor from a UK low-waste home-goods brand, with vegan and cruelty-free positioning.

products.name: MANSCAPED The Plow 2.0

environment.note: The Plow 2.0 is a reusable single-blade safety razor, better on recurring plastic waste than cartridge systems but not explicitly zero-waste positioned.

durability.note: MANSCAPED describes a precision-engineered brass handle and zinc alloy head for the Plow 2.0.

economical.note: The reusable handle and single-blade format lower refill costs compared with proprietary cartridge systems.

ethics.note: MANSCAPED provides a reusable safety-razor option but the product page does not show strong labor, ownership or sustainability certification.

accessibility.note: MANSCAPED has broad brand awareness and direct sales, making this one of the more discoverable mainstream safety-razor entries.

products.description: A mainstream single-blade safety razor that gives cartridge users a recognizable low-waste bridge, with weaker maker-ethics signals.

products.name: Gillette SkinGuard Sensitive

environment.note: SkinGuard uses a reusable handle but still depends on recurring proprietary cartridge refills rather than standard metal blades.

durability.note: The handle can be reused, but the shaving surface is a replaceable two-blade cartridge system.

economical.note: Gillette lists SkinGuard refills as a subscription cartridge product, so ongoing cost stays above standard DE blade packs.

ethics.note: Gillette participates in a TerraCycle razor recycling program, but the default system remains a mixed-material cartridge format.

accessibility.note: Gillette positions SkinGuard for sensitive skin, razor bumps, and shaving irritation, with broad mainstream availability.

products.description: A mainstream sensitive-skin cartridge option: useful for irritation constraints, but still locked into proprietary refills.

products.name: Schick Intuition Sensitive Care

environment.note: Intuition keeps the handle but combines a four-blade cartridge with a built-in moisturizing bar, increasing recurring consumable material.

durability.note: Schick lists refill cartridges for the Intuition system, so the handle persists while the head is repeatedly replaced.

ethics.note: Schick's product-information page provides ingredient and origin details for Intuition refills, but no low-waste or mission certification signal.

accessibility.note: The lather-and-shave-in-one design can reduce setup friction for beginners, travel, or people who find separate shave cream difficult.

products.description: A convenience-first cartridge system that can help people who need lather built in, with weak waste and refill-cost performance.

products.name: DORCO Pace 6 Pro

environment.note: DORCO Pace systems are cartridge razors, so they reduce whole-handle waste compared with disposables but not mixed-material cartridge waste.

durability.note: DORCO sells shaving systems and cartridges across its PACE line rather than a lifetime handle or non-proprietary blade format.

economical.note: Retail listings show Pace 6 Pro multi-cartridge packs priced below many premium cartridge systems, but still above DE blade costs.

ethics.note: DORCO emphasizes long manufacturing history and global blade production, but public sustainability or labor-certification signals are limited.

accessibility.note: DORCO remains available through major online retail, but it is less visible in ordinary drugstore aisles than Gillette or Schick.

products.description: A lower-cost cartridge route for people trying to avoid premium refill prices, not a low-waste shaving system.

products.name: Van Der Hagen 85mm Safety Razor

environment.note: The 85mm razor uses a single double-edge blade rather than proprietary plastic cartridges.

durability.note: Van Der Hagen describes a chrome-plated brass safety razor with a butterfly opening for blade changes.

economical.note: The handle is a low-cost safety-razor bridge and uses standard DE blades, making refills much cheaper than cartridges.

ethics.note: The values case is mostly affordable reusable design; public labor or mission-certification signals were not found.

accessibility.note: The razor is sold through mainstream retailers such as Target and Walmart, making safety-razor trials easier for non-enthusiasts.

products.description: A useful drugstore bridge into safety razors: not a premium heirloom tool, but accessible, cheap to refill, and much lower waste than cartridges.

products.name: Panasonic ARC5 electric shaver

environment.note: An electric shaver avoids disposable wet-shave blades for many users, but adds electronics, battery, foil and cutter replacement impacts.

durability.note: Panasonic sells compatible replacement outer foil and inner blade sets for ARC5 models, supporting maintenance rather than full-device replacement.

economical.note: The ARC5 has a high upfront price and replacement parts, so value depends on replacing years of cartridges or disposable razors.

ethics.note: The public product evidence supports maintenance and reuse, but this is not a mission-led or low-waste certified product.

accessibility.note: Wet/dry electric shaving can be useful for people who need faster, lower-cut-risk, or less ritual-heavy shaving.

products.description: A recognizable premium electric option for people prioritizing speed or irritation control over the lowest-material wet-shave setup.

products.name: Feather Hi-Stainless DE blades

durability.note: These are consumable blades, but the standardized DE format keeps the durable handle independent of one cartridge ecosystem.

economical.note: Feather blades are premium for DE blades but still much cheaper per shave than many cartridge refills.

ethics.note: Feather highlights long-running Japanese replaceable-blade manufacturing, but broad third-party sustainability certification was not found.

accessibility.note: Feather is widely known in wet-shaving shops and online, though less available in ordinary grocery aisles.

products.description: A named premium DE blade choice for safety-razor users who want sharp standard blades without entering a cartridge lock-in.

products.name: Ethique Tip-to-Toe shave bar

environment.note: Ethique describes its bars as plastic-free with home-compostable packaging and a smaller footprint than liquid haircare.

accessibility.note: Ethique is available online and through some retailers, but a bar format may require storage and a different lather routine.

products.description: A solid shave-support product that helps make safety razors practical without aerosol cans or plastic shave-gel bottles.

products.name: Dr. Bronner's Organic Shaving Soap

accessibility.note: Dr. Bronner's is a broadly distributed natural-products brand, making this an easier values-aligned shave-soap swap to find.

products.name: Gillette Fusion5

products.description: A familiar cartridge default: less wasteful than disposable handles, but still locked into plastic-heavy proprietary refills.

products.name: Gillette Mach3

accessibility.note: Mach3 handles and refills remain broadly available through mainstream retail and online channels.

accessibility.note: BIC EasyRinse disposable razors are widely available in US mass retail and online channels.

products.name: Wilkinson Sword Classic Double Edge Razor

products.name: Blade bank / used-blade tin

products.name: Double-edge blade sampler pack

accessibility.note: Sampler packs are easy to buy online but still require comfort with exposed blades and safety-razor technique.

products.name: Philips Norelco Bodygroom route

products.name: Maintained electric trimmer/clipper

accessibility.note: The routine is simple for many users, but it still requires remembering oiling, drying, cleaning, and blade replacement cues.

products.name: Braun Silk-epil epilator

ethics.note: Braun is a mainstream personal-care electronics brand; the product is a reusable route but not a values-certification standout.

accessibility.note: Root-removal can be useful for longer gaps between sessions, but pain tolerance, skin response, and device price make this a selective fit.

products.name: Sugardoh sugaring paste

accessibility.note: Sugaring avoids blades, but technique, pain tolerance, hair length, and skin response make it less universally easy than a familiar razor.

products.name: Veet ready-to-use wax strips

ethics.note: Veet is a mainstream Reckitt brand with limited values-certification signal in this category.

accessibility.note: Veet describes the strips as easy to use for beginners, but the same page lists important use restrictions and skin cautions.

products.description: A convenient mainstream hair-removal floor: easy to find and often cheaper than salon waxing, but strip/wipe waste and skin cautions matter.

products.name: Gillette Foamy aerosol shave foam

ethics.note: This is a mainstream disposable-packaging support product with limited values certification; it is useful as the honest convenience floor.
